hints: Focus on counting how many chlorine atoms are directly bonded to one aluminium atom in each form, that number is the number of bonding pairs.
In $AlCl_3$ the aluminium makes 3 bonds and has no lone pairs, so think what shape 3 pairs gives by VSEPR.
In $Al_2Cl_6$ each aluminium is joined to 2 terminal Cl plus 2 bridging Cl, so use the shape for 4 bonding pairs to complete the pair.
walkthrough:
**Count bonds in $AlCl_3$**

Think simply, how many things are attached to Al? In $AlCl_3$ there are 3 $Al-Cl$ bonds and no lone pairs on Al.

Bonding pairs on Al = 3

**Apply VSEPR to $AlCl_3$**

Three bonding pairs with no lone pairs repel to be as far apart as possible. That is trigonal planar with $120^{\circ}$ angles.

$$3 \text{ bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs} \rightarrow \text{trigonal planar}$$

**Count bonds in $Al_2Cl_6$**

Now picture the dimer. Two $AlCl_3$ units join by two bridging Cl atoms. Each Al is bonded to 2 terminal Cl and 2 bridging Cl.

Bonding pairs on each Al = 4

**Apply VSEPR to $Al_2Cl_6$**

Four bonding pairs with no lone pairs arrange tetrahedrally to minimise repulsion. So the bonding pairs around each Al are tetrahedral.

$$4 \text{ bonding pairs, 0 lone pairs} \rightarrow \text{tetrahedral}$$

options.A: Planar for $AlCl_3$ is right, but planar for $Al_2Cl_6$ is wrong. It forgets the two dative bridging bonds, each Al actually has 4 bonding pairs, not 3.
options.B: Correct. $AlCl_3$ has 3 bonding pairs and 0 lone pairs, giving a trigonal planar arrangement. $Al_2Cl_6$ has 4 bonding pairs around each Al (2 terminal + 2 bridge), giving a tetrahedral arrangement.
options.C: Tetrahedral for $Al_2Cl_6$ is right, but tetrahedral for $AlCl_3$ is wrong. $AlCl_3$ monomer has only 3 bonding pairs, so it cannot be tetrahedral which needs 4 pairs.
options.D: Both are wrong in this option. $AlCl_3$ does not have 4 pairs, and each Al in $Al_2Cl_6$ has only 4 bonds, not 6, so octahedral (which needs 6 pairs) is impossible.
